title: Early warning system coverage for extreme weather
bottleneck: Effective early warnings cut disaster deaths dramatically, yet coverage is grossly unequal: wealthy countries have radar networks, cell broadcast, and evacuation protocols while large parts of Africa, South Asia, and small island states lack even basic weather stations. The WMO estimates a third of the world's population — mostly in least-developed countries — is not covered by early warning systems. Last-mile communication to remote and marginalized communities fails even where forecasts exist.
why_it_blocks: Early warnings are among the most cost-effective climate adaptations, with benefit-cost ratios above 10 to 1, but the coverage gap means the most vulnerable face disasters blind. Every uncovered community is a preventable death toll waiting for the next cyclone or flood.
current_state: The UN's Early Warnings for All initiative targets universal coverage, and low-cost sensors plus mobile networks are extending reach. But funding falls far short, and maintenance of systems in poor regions remains chronically underfunded.
